beats.intro: Chapter two, lesson three. Conjugated and derived proteins. [[bags]]Think of a plain loaf of bread. You can eat it as it is, or you can add something to it: butter, jam, a slice of cheese. The bread is the same, but now it carries a passenger. [[tree]]Here is our protein family tree. Last time we lit the simple proteins, the ones made of amino acids and nothing else. [[lit]]Today we light the other two branches: conjugated proteins, which carry a passenger, and derived proteins, which are what is left after a protein has been changed.
beats.conj: [[def]]A conjugated protein, also called a compound protein, is a protein joined to a non-protein part. The protein part is a chain of amino acids, just as before. The extra part is not made of amino acids at all. [[six]]There are six types, and the easy way to learn them is to ask one question each time: what is the passenger? Carbohydrate, lipid, phosphate, a metal, a pigment, or a nucleic acid.
beats.sugarfat: [[gly]]First, glycoproteins. The passenger is carbohydrate, sugar chains attached to the protein. Examples: the hormones follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone, antibodies, blood-group antigens, receptors, and many enzymes. The slide gives no single function here, because sugar-coated proteins do many jobs. [[lipo]]Second, lipoproteins. The passenger is lipid, fat. Think of a delivery van for fat, because fat does not dissolve in blood. There are four: chylomicrons, very-low-density, low-density and high-density lipoproteins. Their job is to transport lipid in the blood.
beats.phosmetal: [[phos]]Third, phosphoproteins. The passenger is phosphoric acid. The example to remember is caseinogen, the main protein of milk. [[metal]]Fourth, metalloproteins. The passenger is a metal, and there are three to know: copper, zinc and iron. Ceruloplasmin carries and stores copper. Insulin is linked with zinc, and it regulates blood glucose. Transferrin carries iron in the blood, and ferritin stores iron in the cells. Carry, carry, store: copper, iron, iron.
beats.pigment: [[chromo]]Fifth, chromoproteins. Chromo means colour, so the passenger is a pigment. There are two kinds. [[heme]]The red pigment is heme, and proteins that carry it are hemoproteins. Hemoglobin and myoglobin carry oxygen. The cytochromes carry electrons. [[flavin]]The yellow pigment is flavin, and proteins that carry it are flavoproteins. Two flavin carriers, F A D and F M N, carry hydrogen. Red for heme, yellow for flavin.
beats.nucleo: [[nuc]]Sixth, nucleoproteins. The passenger is a nucleic acid, D N A or R N A. Remember the histones from last lesson? [[chromosome]]A chromosome is histone protein packed with D N A. [[ribosome]]A ribosome is protein plus R N A. Like the glycoproteins, the slide gives examples but no single function. That makes six conjugated types, each with its own passenger.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which conjugated protein has iron or copper as its non-protein part?
beats.derived: [[def]]Now the third branch, the derived proteins. These are not built from anything. They are what you get when a simple or a conjugated protein is changed, either by denaturation or by hydrolysis. [[two]]And there are two groups, depending on what happened to the peptide bonds. Primary derived proteins, and secondary derived proteins.
beats.primary: [[egg]]Primary derived proteins come from denaturation. Heat is the usual denaturing agent. Think of an egg white turning solid in a hot pan. [[chain]]The slide shows the protein turning into protean, and then into metaprotein, the coagulated protein. The shape is changed, but no peptide bond is broken, and the molecular weight does not change. [[ex]]The examples are coagulated albumin and coagulated globulin. Same chain, new shape. We will meet denaturation properly in chapter three.
beats.secondary: [[hyd]]Secondary derived proteins come from hydrolysis, using hydrolysing agents such as enzymes. Think of a protein meal being digested. Here the peptide bonds really do break, and the molecular weight falls. [[steps]]The chain runs in order: protein, then proteoses, then peptones, then peptides, and finally amino acids. At each step the pieces get smaller. [[mw]]The slide calls this progressive hydrolysis of the peptide bond. The molecular weight keeps falling until we reach single amino acids, the units we started with in chapter one.
beats.q2: Quick check. Heat turns an egg white solid, but no peptide bond is broken. Is the result a primary or a secondary derived protein?
beats.compare: [[side]]Let's put them side by side. Primary: denaturation, a denaturing agent such as heat, peptide bonds stay, molecular weight unchanged. Secondary: hydrolysis, a hydrolysing agent such as an enzyme, peptide bonds break, molecular weight falls. [[trick]]A quick test: did the chain get cut? If not, primary. If it did, secondary.
beats.tree: [[full]]Now our family tree is complete. Proteins divide into three branches. Simple proteins, made of amino acids only. Conjugated proteins, with a passenger: carbohydrate, lipid, phosphate, a metal, a pigment, or a nucleic acid. [[derived]]And derived proteins, the products of denaturation or hydrolysis. [[end]]Every protein you meet in this course will sit on one of these branches.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Conjugated proteins are a protein plus a non-protein part. There are six types, named by the passenger: glyco, lipo, phospho, metallo, chromo and nucleo. [[s2]]Metalloproteins carry copper, zinc and iron. Chromoproteins carry the red pigment heme or the yellow pigment flavin. [[s3]]Derived proteins come from denaturation, the primary group, where no peptide bond breaks, or from hydrolysis, the secondary group, where the chain is cut down to amino acids. [[end]]Now try the practice.
